segments.caption: 5 ways the Central Limit Theorem runs the real world.
Election polls, A/B tests, factories, insurance, and machine learning. Save this one!
Quick recap. Take many samples and average each one.
Even if the data is skewed, those averages form a bell curve.
And their spread, the standard error, is sigma over root n. More data, a narrower bell.
Use one: election polls.
A pollster asks 1,000 voters out of millions. Each answer is just yes or no, nowhere near a bell curve.
But the share saying yes is an average, so it's roughly normal. That's why 52% ±3% is a real 95% range.
And to halve that margin, you need 4 times the people: 4,000 voters gives ±1.5%.
Use two: A/B tests.
Customer spending is very skewed: most people spend a little, and a few spend a lot.
But the average spend over thousands of users is normal. That's why a simple z or t test can compare version A with version B.
Use three: factories.
Every hour, a juice plant weighs 5 bottles and plots their average on a control chart.
The averages stay within 3 standard errors, 99.7% of the time. A point outside the lines means: stop the machine.
Use four: insurance.
One customer's claims are unpredictable: nothing for years, then one huge claim.
But across 100,000 customers, the average claim is very predictable. Its standard error shrinks about 300 times. That's how premiums are set.
Use five: machine learning.
A model scores 90% accuracy on 1,000 test examples. Each prediction is just right or wrong.
But accuracy is an average, so it's roughly normal, with a standard error of about 1%. The true accuracy is about 88 to 92%.
Test on 10,000 examples, and the range tightens to about ±0.6%.
See the pattern? The raw data is messy, but averages behave. That's why the bell curve shows up everywhere.
In fact, every z-test, t-test, and confidence interval on this page leans on this one theorem.
Two interview traps.
One: the theorem is about averages, not the data. Individual values stay skewed.
Two: it needs independent samples and enough data: about 30 for mild skew, far more for heavy tails like incomes.
